definition: A signal defined for every value of a real time variable, usually written x(t).
wrongs: A sequence defined only at integer time indexes.
A count of how many pixels share one gray level.
A file split stored on one cluster node.
why: Time is a continuous variable, so the signal has a value at every real instant, not only at integers.
example: A microphone voltage recorded as a smooth waveform x(t) before any sampler runs.
scenario: An oscilloscope trace has a voltage at every real instant, not only at integer ticks. Which signal class is displayed?
scenarioWhy: A value at every real time is a continuous-time signal.

definition: A sequence defined only at integer time indexes, usually written x[n].
wrongs: A waveform defined for every real value of time.
A periodic impulse train used only as a sampler.
The phase angle of a frequency response.
why: The index n takes integer values, so there is no requirement to define the signal between those indexes.
example: Daily closing temperatures form a sequence x[n] with one sample per day.
scenario: A processor stores one temperature per integer hour and has no values between hours. Which signal class is stored?
scenarioWhy: A sequence indexed by integers is a discrete-time signal.

definition: Recording a continuous-time signal at evenly spaced instants to form a discrete-time sequence.
wrongs: Adding two sequences to test linearity.
Integrating a signal against a complex exponential over all time.
Holding each sample constant until the next sample without taking new values.
why: Each sample is the continuous waveform at time n times the sampling period, which produces x[n].
example: An audio interface reads a microphone voltage 44100 times each second.
scenario: An engineer measures a sensor voltage every 1 millisecond and stores only those readings. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Taking evenly spaced readings of a continuous waveform is sampling.

definition: Twice the highest frequency of a bandlimited signal, which the sampling rate must exceed for exact reconstruction.
wrongs: Half the sampling frequency, the highest frequency a given sampler can represent.
The cutoff of a low-pass filter already built in hardware.
The fundamental period of a repeating waveform.
why: Sampling theory sets the threshold rate at two times the highest frequency present.
example: A voice limited to 4 kHz has a Nyquist rate of 8 kHz.
scenario: A signal contains nothing above 5 kHz. Which sampling rate is exactly the Nyquist rate for it?
scenarioWhy: Twice the highest frequency, 2 times 5 kHz, is the Nyquist rate.

definition: Half the sampling frequency, which is the highest frequency that sampling rate can represent.
wrongs: Twice the highest frequency in the original continuous signal.
The spacing in seconds between successive samples.
The area under an impulse response.
why: Frequencies above half the sampling rate fold, so that half-rate is the representation limit.
example: Audio sampled at 44100 Hz has a Nyquist frequency of 22050 Hz.
scenario: A converter samples at 8 kHz. Which frequency is its Nyquist frequency?
scenarioWhy: Half of the 8 kHz sampling rate is 4 kHz.

definition: The appearance of frequencies above half the sampling rate as false lower frequencies.
wrongs: Perfect recovery of a bandlimited signal by ideal low-pass interpolation.
A time shift of the output that exactly matches a shift of the input.
A pole moving deeper into the left half of the s-plane.
why: When sampling is too slow, repeated spectra overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones.
example: A 9 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz shows up in the samples as a 1 kHz tone.
scenario: A 9 kHz whistle sampled at 10 kHz is heard as 1 kHz. Which effect occurred?
scenarioWhy: A high tone folding into a lower tone because sampling was too slow is aliasing.

definition: A bandlimited signal can be reconstructed exactly if it is sampled faster than twice its highest frequency.
wrongs: Any signal, even one with unlimited bandwidth, can be rebuilt from two samples.
Sampling slower than the highest frequency always improves reconstruction.
A zero-order hold is the ideal reconstructor named by the theorem.
why: Above that rate the spectral copies do not overlap, so a low-pass interpolator can isolate the original.
example: Music bandlimited to 20 kHz is captured at 48 kHz, which is fast enough for exact reconstruction in theory.
scenario: A signal is bandlimited to 3 kHz and sampled at 8 kHz. Does the sampling theorem allow exact reconstruction?
scenarioWrongs: No, because the rate must be below 3 kHz
Yes, but only if the rate is exactly 3 kHz
No, because only periodic signals can be reconstructed
scenarioWhy: The sampling rate is higher than twice the highest frequency, so the theorem says reconstruction is possible.

definition: The central Signal and Systems model: a system that is both linear and time-invariant.
wrongs: A system that multiplies the input by a changing gain that depends on absolute time.
A system that adds a fixed offset so doubling the input does not double the output.
A sampler that keeps only every tenth sample of a sequence.
why: Signal and Systems treats an LTI system as linear and time-invariant, so its output is the input convolved with one impulse response.
example: An RC low-pass filter obeys superposition and responds the same way whenever the same pulse arrives.
scenario: A filter obeys superposition, and delaying its input only delays its output by the same amount. Which model applies?
scenarioWrongs: An adder with a constant offset
scenarioWhy: Linearity plus time invariance is exactly the LTI model used in Signal and Systems.

definition: The property that a scaled sum of inputs produces the same scaled sum of outputs.
wrongs: The property that a time shift of the input only shifts the output.
The property that the output ignores all past inputs.
The property that every bounded input produces an unbounded output.
why: Both additivity and homogeneity are required, which together are the superposition rule.
example: If a circuit turns x1 into y1 and x2 into y2, then 3 x1 plus 2 x2 must produce 3 y1 plus 2 y2.
scenario: Doubling an audio input doubles the output, and the response to a sum is the sum of responses. Which property holds?
scenarioWhy: Scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs, which is linearity.

definition: The property that shifting the input in time shifts the output by the same amount and changes nothing else.
wrongs: The property that a sum of inputs produces the sum of outputs.
The property that the impulse response is zero for negative time.
The property that energy over all time is finite.
why: The system rule does not depend on the absolute clock time at which the input is applied.
example: A fixed echo unit delays any clap by 50 milliseconds, whether the clap is at noon or later.
scenario: A processor behaves the same at every hour: delaying the input by 4 samples delays the output by 4 samples. Which property is that?
scenarioWhy: A pure delay of the output when the input is delayed is time invariance.

definition: Combining an input with an impulse response by flip, slide, and sum, which gives the output of an LTI system.
wrongs: Multiplying two Fourier transforms point by point with no time-domain interpretation.
Sampling a waveform at twice its highest frequency.
Setting every negative-time sample of a sequence to zero by hand.
why: For a discrete LTI system the output sample is the sum over k of x[k] times h[n-k].
example: A short echo kernel is flipped and slid across a recorded clap to produce the echoed clap.
scenario: Students compute each output sample as the sum over k of x[k] times h[n-k]. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: That sum is the convolution of the input with the impulse response.

definition: The output of a system when the input is a unit impulse at the origin.
wrongs: The steady gain and phase at one sinusoid frequency only.
The list of denominator roots of a transfer function.
The band of frequencies a filter is meant to block.
why: An LTI system is completely described by this response, because every input is a combination of impulses.
example: A single click sent into a reverb pedal produces the decaying tail that is stored as h[n].
scenario: A lab applies a unit sample at n = 0 and records the output sequence. What has been measured?
scenarioWrongs: The frequency response at one tone
scenarioWhy: The output caused by a unit impulse is the impulse response.

definition: The complex gain an LTI system applies at each frequency, equal to the Fourier transform of its impulse response.
wrongs: The time waveform produced by a unit impulse.
The region of the s-plane where a Laplace integral converges.
The average power of a periodic input.
why: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems, and the eigenvalue at each frequency is this response.
example: A tone at 1 kHz leaves a filter louder and slightly delayed, as predicted by H at that frequency.
scenario: A lab sweeps a sine wave and records the output amplitude and phase at each frequency. Which function is being measured?
scenarioWhy: Gain and phase versus frequency form the frequency response.

definition: A representation of a periodic signal as a sum of harmonically related sinusoids.
wrongs: An integral transform used for a one-time aperiodic pulse.
A sum of x[n] times powers of z.
A differential equation relating input and output derivatives.
why: A periodic signal repeats, so its spectrum sits on discrete harmonic frequencies of the fundamental.
example: A clarinet note is written as a fundamental plus weaker harmonics at integer multiples of that pitch.
scenario: A square wave repeats every 2 milliseconds and is expanded into a fundamental and its harmonics. Which representation is that?
scenarioWrongs: A continuous-time Fourier transform of a pulse
scenarioWhy: Harmonics of a periodic waveform are its Fourier series.

definition: An integral that expresses an aperiodic continuous-time signal as complex exponentials over all frequencies.
wrongs: A discrete harmonic sum used only for periodic signals.
A sum over integer n of x[n] times powers of a complex z.
A count of samples taken in one second.
why: The continuous-time Fourier transform integrates x(t) against complex exponentials to obtain a frequency function X(jw).
example: A single rectangular pulse, which does not repeat, has a sinc-shaped continuous spectrum.
scenario: A non-repeating pulse is analyzed by integrating it against complex exponentials over all time. Which transform is that?
scenarioWhy: The integral frequency analysis of an aperiodic continuous signal is the Fourier transform.

definition: A sum that writes a discrete-time signal as complex exponentials over a continuous frequency interval of length 2 pi.
wrongs: An integral over real t used only for continuous-time waveforms.
A harmonic series that requires the time signal to be periodic.
A Laplace integral that includes a real decay factor in s.
why: The transform sums x[n] exp(-j w n), and the result repeats every 2 pi because n is an integer.
example: A five-sample discrete pulse has a DTFT that is a smooth function of frequency and repeats every 2 pi.
scenario: Students sum x[n] exp(-j w n) over n and obtain a spectrum that repeats every 2 pi. Which transform did they compute?
scenarioWhy: That sum, periodic in frequency with period 2 pi, is the discrete-time Fourier transform.

definition: An integral of x(t) times an exponential decay in the complex variable s, used to solve continuous LTI systems.
wrongs: A sum of a discrete sequence times powers of z.
A purely imaginary-frequency integral that cannot place poles in the s-plane.
A time-domain flip-and-slide of two sequences.
why: The factor exp(-s t) lets the transform converge for unstable or growing signals inside a region of convergence and exposes poles.
example: The charging curve of a capacitor is transformed in s so a differential equation becomes algebra.
scenario: A continuous circuit equation is solved by transforming x(t) into a function of complex s. Which transform is used?
scenarioWhy: Continuous-time signals transformed in the complex variable s use the Laplace transform.

definition: A sum of the sequence x[n] times z to the power -n, the discrete-time counterpart of the Laplace transform.
wrongs: An integral of a continuous waveform against exp(-s t).
A harmonic sum that requires the waveform to repeat in time.
A running average of neighboring pixels.
why: Powers of z replace the continuous exponential, and the region of convergence decides which sequence the transform represents.
example: A geometric sequence a to the n, for n at least 0, has a z-transform that is a simple rational function.
scenario: A discrete recurrence is solved by summing x[n] z to the -n. Which transform is that?
scenarioWhy: The power series in z of a discrete sequence is the z-transform.

definition: The set of complex s or z values for which a Laplace or z-transform sum or integral converges.
wrongs: The passband of a low-pass filter.
The set of time instants where a signal is nonzero.
The list of numerator roots of a transfer function.
why: Without the region, a rational transform can correspond to more than one time signal.
example: The transform 1 over (1 - 2 z inverse) can be a right-sided or left-sided sequence depending on the region.
scenario: Two different sequences share the same rational z-transform expression. What extra information separates them?
scenarioWhy: The region of convergence selects which time signal a rational transform represents.

definition: The ratio of the output transform to the input transform for an LTI system that starts at rest.
wrongs: The time signal produced by a unit impulse, written as a sequence.
The sampling period measured in seconds.
The average power of a sinusoid that has lasted forever.
why: With zero initial conditions, Y(s) equals H(s) times X(s), so H(s) is that ratio, and likewise for H(z).
example: A resting RC filter has H(s) equal to 1 over (1 plus R C s).
scenario: With zero initial conditions, the Laplace transform of the output divided by that of the input is formed. What is that ratio called?
scenarioWhy: The output-over-input transform of a resting LTI system is its transfer function.

definition: A denominator root of a transfer function, where the response magnitude is unbounded.
wrongs: A numerator root where the transfer function is zero.
A frequency that a low-pass filter is designed to pass.
A sample index where a unit step first becomes 1.
why: The denominator vanishes at a pole and the numerator does not, so the transfer function goes to infinity there.
example: A system H(s) = 1 over (s plus 2) has a single pole at s = -2.
scenario: H(s) blows up at s = -3 and the denominator is zero there. What is s = -3 called?
scenarioWhy: A denominator root where the transfer function is unbounded is a pole.

definition: A numerator root of a transfer function, where that factor contributes no output.
wrongs: A denominator root where the transfer function is unbounded.
The time at which an impulse response starts.
Half the sampling frequency of a converter.
why: The numerator is zero while the denominator is not, so the transfer function itself is zero at that point.
example: H(z) = 1 minus z inverse has a zero at z = 1, so it rejects a constant input.
scenario: A filter's transfer function is exactly zero at z = -1, canceling a Nyquist-rate oscillation. What is z = -1 called?
scenarioWhy: A numerator root that forces the transfer function to zero is a zero.

definition: A filter that passes frequencies below a cutoff and attenuates frequencies above that cutoff.
wrongs: A filter that blocks low frequencies and passes high ones.
A filter that passes only a middle band and blocks both low and high ends.
A filter that passes every frequency with the same gain.
why: Its passband sits next to zero frequency and its stopband occupies the high frequencies.
example: A hi-fi rumble filter keeps bass and midrange but weakens a 20 kHz hiss.
scenario: A designer wants to keep speech under 4 kHz and weaken everything above it. Which filter type is required?
scenarioWhy: Passing the low band and attenuating the high band is low-pass behavior.

definition: A filter that attenuates frequencies below a cutoff and passes frequencies above it.
wrongs: A filter that keeps low frequencies and removes high ones.
A filter that keeps only a narrow middle band.
A filter whose impulse response is a unit step.
why: The stopband includes zero frequency and the passband lies above the cutoff.
example: An audio high-pass removes a 50 Hz hum while leaving a 2 kHz flute note intact.
scenario: A recording must lose a low rumble but keep bright cymbal frequencies. Which filter type fits?
scenarioWhy: Attenuating lows and passing highs is high-pass behavior.

definition: A filter that passes frequencies between a lower and an upper cutoff and attenuates the rest.
wrongs: A filter that passes only frequencies near zero.
A filter that passes everything above one cutoff.
A filter that stops a middle band and passes both extremes.
why: Two cutoffs bound a single passband that does not include zero frequency or the extreme highs.
example: A radio tuner keeps a station around 98 MHz and rejects both lower and higher channels.
scenario: A receiver must keep 300 Hz to 3 kHz and reject both lower and higher frequencies. Which filter type is that?
scenarioWhy: A single middle passband bounded by two cutoffs is band-pass.

definition: The property that the output at any time depends only on the input at that time and earlier times.
wrongs: The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output.
The property that the system may use future input samples.
The property that a sinusoid passes through unchanged in shape.
why: For an LTI system this is equivalent to the impulse response being zero before time zero.
example: A real-time speaker can react to a clap only after the clap, never before it happens.
scenario: An LTI impulse response h[n] is zero for every negative n. Which property does that guarantee?
scenarioWhy: An impulse response that is zero for negative time means the system is causal.

definition: The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output.
wrongs: The property that the output never depends on future inputs.
The property that the system has no memory of past inputs.
The property that the frequency response is identically 1.
why: An LTI system is BIBO stable exactly when its impulse response is absolutely integrable or absolutely summable.
example: A decaying exponential impulse response stays absolutely summable, so a bounded tone cannot make the output explode.
scenario: Every input that stays within a finite amplitude produces an output that also stays finite. Which property is that?
scenarioWhy: Bounded inputs yielding bounded outputs is the definition of BIBO stability.

definition: The discrete signal that equals 1 at index 0 and equals 0 at every other integer index.
wrongs: The signal that is 0 before time zero and 1 afterward.
A periodic train of impulses spaced by the sampling period.
A constant sequence equal to 1 at every index.
why: That single 1 at the origin is the discrete unit sample used to probe an LTI system.
example: A test sequence contains a 1 at n = 0 and zeros at all other stored indexes.
scenario: A test vector is 1 at n = 0 and 0 at every other n. Which standard signal is it?
scenarioWhy: A lone 1 at index 0 is the discrete unit impulse.

definition: A signal that is 0 before time zero and 1 at time zero and afterward.
wrongs: A signal that is 1 only at time zero and 0 elsewhere.
A signal that flips sign when time is reversed.
A signal that repeats every fixed period T.
why: The step turns on at the origin and stays on, which is the discrete or continuous unit step.
example: A switch applies 1 volt at t = 0 and holds that voltage for all later time.
scenario: A sequence is 0 for negative n and 1 for n = 0, 1, 2, and so on. Which standard signal is it?
scenarioWhy: Turning on at time zero and staying at 1 is the unit step.

definition: A signal that is unchanged by time reversal, so its value at -t equals its value at t.
wrongs: A signal that changes sign under time reversal.
A signal that is zero for all negative time.
A signal whose total energy is infinite.
why: Symmetry about the origin means the waveform on the left is a mirror of the waveform on the right.
example: A cosine wave has the same voltage at time -t as at time t.
scenario: A waveform satisfies x(-t) = x(t) for every t. Which symmetry does it have?
scenarioWhy: Equality with its time reverse is even symmetry.

definition: A signal that flips sign under time reversal, so its value at -t is the negative of its value at t.
wrongs: A signal that matches itself under time reversal.
A signal that repeats every T seconds.
A signal with finite nonzero average power.
why: The left side is an upside-down copy of the right side, which forces the value at time zero to be 0 for an ordinary function.
example: A sine wave at time -t is the negative of the sine wave at time t.
scenario: A waveform satisfies x(-t) = -x(t) for every t. Which symmetry does it have?
scenarioWhy: A sign flip under time reversal is odd symmetry.

definition: A signal that repeats exactly after some fixed positive interval T, for every time.
wrongs: A one-shot pulse that is zero outside a finite interval.
A signal whose squared magnitude sums to a finite energy.
A signal that is zero before a start time and never repeats.
why: There exists T greater than 0 such that shifting the signal by T leaves it unchanged.
example: A clock square wave looks identical after every 1 millisecond shift.
scenario: Shifting a waveform by 4 milliseconds leaves it identical, and 4 milliseconds is the smallest such shift. Which property is this?
scenarioWhy: Exact repetition after a fixed interval means the signal is periodic.

definition: A signal whose total energy, the sum or integral of its squared magnitude, is finite.
wrongs: A signal with finite nonzero average power and infinite duration.
A forever sinusoid of constant amplitude.
A periodic square wave that has always been running.
why: Finite energy usually means the signal dies out, so its average power over infinite time is zero.
example: A single finite-length beep has finite energy and then stays at zero.
scenario: A pulse is nonzero for only 20 milliseconds and its squared area is finite. Which energy-power class is it?
scenarioWhy: Finite total squared magnitude means the pulse is an energy signal.

definition: A signal with finite nonzero average power, which implies that its total energy is infinite.
wrongs: A finite-length pulse whose squared magnitude integrates to a finite number.
The zero signal, whose power and energy are both zero.
A signal that is undefined at integer times only.
why: Persistent signals such as everlasting sinusoids spread infinite energy over infinite time but keep a finite average power.
example: A sine wave that has always been on and never ends has finite average power and infinite energy.
scenario: An everlasting cosine has a finite average of its squared value and infinite total energy. Which class is it?
scenarioWrongs: A signal undefined on the integers
scenarioWhy: Finite nonzero average power with infinite energy is a power signal.

definition: A reconstruction that keeps each sample value constant until the next sample instant.
wrongs: Ideal bandlimited interpolation that uses sinc functions.
Sampling that only records values and does not rebuild a waveform.
A high-order polynomial fit through many future samples.
why: Between sampling instants the output is a flat step equal to the most recent sample.
example: A digital-to-analog pin holds 0.5 volts steady until the next code arrives and the level jumps.
scenario: Between samples a converter output stays flat at the last sample value. Which reconstructor is that?
scenarioWhy: Holding the latest sample constant until the next one is a zero-order hold.

definition: The phase angle of the frequency response, showing the phase shift at each frequency.
wrongs: The magnitude of the frequency response, showing only gain.
The impulse response written as a time sequence.
The list of poles in the left half-plane.
why: The frequency response is complex, and its argument is the phase shift applied to a complex exponential.
example: At 1 kHz a filter leaves the tone amplitude unchanged but delays the peaks by a quarter cycle.
scenario: A tone's amplitude is unchanged, but its peaks are shifted by a quarter cycle. Which part of the frequency response captures that shift?
scenarioWhy: Phase shift versus frequency is the phase response.

definition: The negative slope of the phase response with respect to frequency, giving the delay of a narrowband envelope.
wrongs: The phase angle itself at a single frequency.
The cutoff where power gain has fallen by half.
The sampling period in seconds.
why: A narrowband packet is delayed by the negative derivative of phase, not merely by the phase divided by frequency.
example: A short radio burst centered at 10 kHz is delayed by 2 milliseconds, matching the local phase slope.
scenario: Engineers estimate the delay of a narrowband pulse envelope from the slope of phase versus frequency. Which quantity is that?
scenarioWhy: Envelope delay from the negative phase slope is group delay.

definition: The fact that a complex exponential input to an LTI system emerges scaled by the frequency response.
wrongs: The fact that every input, of any shape, is unchanged by an LTI system.
The fact that convolution in time becomes convolution in frequency.
The fact that a unit step input produces a unit step output.
why: Exponentials pass through LTI systems as the same exponential multiplied by H at that frequency.
example: A complex tone exp(j w t) enters a filter and leaves as H(jw) times the same tone.
scenario: A complex exponential enters an LTI filter and exits as the same exponential times a complex constant. Which property explains that?
scenarioWhy: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems, scaled by the frequency response.

definition: An equation linking a continuous output and its derivatives to the input and the input derivatives.
wrongs: A relation among a few discrete samples of an input and output sequence.
A sum of harmonically related sinusoids.
A statement that the output ignores all past inputs.
why: Linear constant-coefficient differential equations are the continuous-time models whose transfer functions are rational in s.
example: The RC circuit law R C dy/dt plus y equals x relates capacitor voltage to the source.
scenario: A circuit is described by R C dy/dt plus y equals the source voltage. Which model form is that?
scenarioWhy: A relation involving a continuous derivative of the output is a differential equation model.

definition: An equation that writes an output sample using a finite number of past inputs and past outputs.
wrongs: An equation that uses derivatives of a continuous waveform.
An integral definition of a Fourier transform.
A requirement that sampling exceed twice the highest frequency.
why: Constant-coefficient difference equations are the discrete-time models with rational transfer functions in z.
example: A smoother sets y[n] equal to 0.5 y[n-1] plus 0.5 x[n].
scenario: A program computes each y[n] from y[n-1] and x[n] with fixed coefficients. Which equation type is that?
scenarioWhy: Relating discrete samples with fixed delays is a difference equation.

definition: Multiplying a continuous signal by a periodic train of impulses to mark weighted sample values.
wrongs: Holding each sample constant between sampling instants.
Adding a unit step to a signal to test stability.
Convolving a signal with a low-pass impulse response.
why: Each impulse picks out the signal value at one sampling instant, which is the ideal model of uniform sampling.
example: A 1 kHz sine is multiplied by impulses spaced every 0.1 millisecond to form weighted spikes.
scenario: A textbook models sampling by multiplying x(t) by a periodic train of impulses. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: Multiplication by a periodic impulse train is the impulse-train sampling model.

definition: Ideal reconstruction that replaces each sample by a sinc pulse and sums those pulses.
wrongs: Holding each sample flat until the next sample.
Repeating the spectrum without low-pass filtering.
Quantizing amplitudes to the nearest integer level.
why: When the sampling theorem holds, the sinc sum equals the original bandlimited continuous signal.
example: Samples of a bandlimited tone are each replaced by a sinc and added to redraw the smooth tone.
scenario: Reconstruction sums shifted sinc pulses weighted by the samples of a properly sampled tone. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: The ideal bandlimited reconstructor is a sum of sinc pulses.

definition: The frequency at the edge of a filter passband, often where the power gain has fallen to half.
wrongs: The sampling rate itself.
The fundamental period of the input.
The location of a zero that has no effect on the passband edge.
why: The cutoff marks the boundary between the frequencies the filter is intended to pass and those it starts to reject.
example: An RC low-pass is quoted with a cutoff of 1 kHz, near the half-power point of its curve.
scenario: A low-pass specification names 2 kHz as the edge where power gain is about half. Which specification number is that?
scenarioWhy: The half-power edge of the passband is a cutoff frequency.

definition: The band of frequencies a filter is intended to transmit with little attenuation.
wrongs: The band a filter is intended to attenuate strongly.
The set of poles in the right half-plane.
The time support of a causal impulse response.
why: Inside the passband the magnitude response stays close to the desired gain.
example: A speech low-pass treats 0 to 3.4 kHz as the band that should come through clearly.
scenario: A spec says frequencies from 0 to 1 kHz must be transmitted with almost no loss. What is that frequency interval called?
scenarioWhy: The interval meant to pass with little loss is the passband.

definition: The band of frequencies a filter is intended to attenuate strongly.
wrongs: The band a filter is intended to pass with little loss.
The region of convergence of a transform.
The set of sample indexes where a unit impulse is 1.
why: Inside the stopband the magnitude response is kept below a required attenuation.
example: A speech low-pass treats frequencies above 4.6 kHz as the band that should be heavily reduced.
scenario: A low-pass spec demands strong attenuation above 8 kHz. What is that high-frequency interval called?
scenarioWhy: The interval that must be strongly attenuated is the stopband.

definition: The result that convolution of two time signals becomes multiplication of their Fourier transforms.
wrongs: The result that convolution in time becomes convolution in frequency.
The result that addition in time becomes multiplication in frequency.
The result that sampling in time erases the frequency content.
why: Filtering an input is convolution with h in time and multiplication by H in frequency.
example: Multiplying a speech spectrum by a low-pass H is equivalent to convolving the speech with h(t).
scenario: An engineer multiplies a spectrum by H(jw) instead of convolving the waveform with h(t). Which theorem justifies that shortcut?
scenarioWrongs: A claim that convolution stays convolution in frequency
A claim that addition becomes multiplication
A claim that sampling removes all frequencies
scenarioWhy: Time-domain convolution corresponds to multiplication of Fourier transforms.

definition: A system whose output at a time depends only on the input at that same time.
wrongs: A system whose output depends on past inputs through an energy-storage element.
A system that needs future samples to form the current output.
A system that convolves the input with a long impulse response.
why: No stored energy or past sample is required, so a resistor obeying Ohm's law is memoryless while a capacitor is not.
example: A resistor sets voltage equal to resistance times the current at the same instant.
scenario: An output sample y[n] equals 3 times x[n] and uses no other sample. Which system class is that?
scenarioWrongs: A noncausal averager of future samples
scenarioWhy: Dependence on only the current input means the system is memoryless.

definition: The condition that the sum of the absolute values of a discrete impulse response is finite.
wrongs: The condition that a continuous signal repeats every T seconds.
The condition that a pole lies in the right half of the s-plane.
The condition that the sampling rate is below the Nyquist rate.
why: For a discrete-time LTI system, a finite sum of absolute impulse-response values is necessary and sufficient for BIBO stability.
example: A sequence equal to one-half raised to n, for every n at least 0, has absolute values that sum to 2.
scenario: The absolute values of h[n] sum to a finite number. What does that imply for the discrete LTI system?
scenarioWrongs: It must be sampled too slowly
scenarioWhy: Absolute summability of h[n] is the BIBO stability test for discrete LTI systems.

definition: A signal that is identically zero before some finite start time.
wrongs: A signal that is identically zero after some finite stop time.
A signal that is nonzero for both large positive and large negative time.
A signal that repeats and so has no start time.
why: Its nonzero part lies at and to the right of a start time on the time axis.
example: A causal exponential is zero for negative time and nonzero afterward, so it is right-sided.
scenario: A Laplace transform is known to come from a signal that is zero before t = 0. Which support class is that signal?
scenarioWhy: Being zero before a finite start time makes the signal right-sided.

definition: The Laplace integral taken from time zero forward, used for causal signals and initial conditions.
wrongs: The two-sided integral from negative infinity to positive infinity.
A sum of a discrete sequence against powers of z.
A Fourier series of a periodic wave.
